name: N,alpha-diethylphenylethylamine (Craze)

lead: N,alpha-diethylphenethylamine (DEPEA) is a stimulant related to methamphetamine. It became known when it was found in pre-workout supplements, including one sold as Craze, in 2013.

People took the supplements for training energy and focus. In appearance terms, the claimed chain is more intense training and an easier diet, which supports muscle and leanness. The compound itself has never been tested in humans.

paras: It was consumed inside pre-workout powders, where it appeared in the label under a different name (Dendrobium extract). Users did not choose it as a known compound. Information about dose or use is not given here.

Animal work shows a stimulant effect, and the substance has not been studied in humans. It is controlled in several countries, including Class A in the UK and Schedule I in Canada. New Zealand issued a warning over Craze in 2013.

lead: N,alpha-diethylphenethylamine (DEPEA, also written N,alpha-ETH, NADEP or EAPB, and chemically 2-ethylamino-1-phenylbutane) is a stimulant of the phenylisobutylamine group and a close structural analogue of methamphetamine. Knoll Pharma originally patented it with related compounds for pharmaceutical use, but none was developed into a medicine.[1] It reached lifters not as a product people chose but as an ingredient in pre-workout supplements, where it was sold for training energy and focus.[1][2]

The appearance link is the one that users of such products describe: more energy and focus for training sessions and diet phases, with the hoped-for chain of harder workouts, easier appetite control, and over time more muscle and less fat. No study has tested that chain, and the compound has never been tested in humans.[1][2] Its story comes from analytical chemistry and regulation: in 2013 it was identified in the supplements Craze (Driven Sports) and Detonate (Gaspari Nutrition), listed on labels under a different name, Dendrobium extract.[1]

Researchers have since measured how much of it supplements contain, found it in human urine, characterised its action in rat tissue, and tested it in rodents. In rats it raises blood pressure and is roughly ten times weaker than amphetamine in producing locomotor stimulation, and a 2022 self-administration study suggested possible abuse potential.[3][4] It is a controlled substance in the UK (Class A), Canada (Schedule I) and New Zealand (Class C), and is listed in Germany's NpSG.[1]

paras: DEPEA has the formula C12H19N and a molar mass of about 177.3 g/mol. Its IUPAC name is N-ethyl-1-phenylbutan-2-amine, and it belongs to the alpha-ethylphenethylamine group, in which an ethyl group sits on the alpha carbon of the phenethylamine backbone and a second ethyl group on the nitrogen. Wikipedia describes it as a close analogue of methamphetamine.[1]

Because several positional isomers share the formula, analysts have had to separate them. A 2015 LC-MS-MS study developed methods to distinguish N,alpha-ETH from its N,beta isomer and re-analysed supplement samples previously reported to contain N,alpha-ETH, confirming that only the N,alpha isomer was present.[5] A 2014 method paper from the same laboratory screened supplements for the compound and related amines.[6]

Pharmacology work indicates a mixed norepinephrine and dopamine releasing agent and reuptake inhibitor.[1] A 2021 study of rat brain tissue and rats found DEPEA to be a full norepinephrine releaser but only a weak partial dopamine releaser, with a maximal efficacy of about 40 percent; in rats the alpha-ethylphenethylamine analogues raised blood pressure and were roughly ten times less potent than amphetamine.[3][1] Other studies reported no dopamine release in cell culture or striatal slice experiments.[1] It is a low-potency TAAR1 agonist in rats and inactive at mouse and human TAAR1 at the concentrations tested.[1]

A 2014 enzyme study found DEPEA to be a weak inhibitor of both forms of monoamine oxidase,[7] and a 2016 screen of 27 amine stimulants listed it among several moderate inhibitors of the liver enzyme CYP2D6, raising the possibility of interactions with other substances.[8] In a 2022 self-administration experiment, male rats self-administered DEPEA and a related analogue with inverted dose-response curves peaking at an intermediate dose, which the authors read as a sign these ingredients may carry abuse potential.[4]
The compound has not been studied in humans. Pieter Cohen of Harvard Medical School has said he expects it to be less potent than methamphetamine but more potent than ephedrine.[1]

Knoll Pharma patented DEPEA together with related analogues for pharmaceutical use; animal studies of those analogues reported cognitive enhancement and increased pain tolerance, but none became a medicine.[1]

In January 2013 South Korean researchers reported identifying the compound in a crystalline powder seized for suspected drug trafficking and predicted it would reach the market.[1] Later in 2013 it was found in biologically significant amounts in two pre-workout supplements, Craze and Detonate, falsely labelled as Dendrobium extract.[1] A paper by Lee and colleagues quantified it in pre-workout supplements sold over the internet.[1]

Cohen, Travis and Venhuis reported in Drug Testing and Analysis (2014) that after athletes had been disqualified for doping, three lots of Craze were tested; two laboratories identified the compound, confirmed by nuclear magnetic resonance and reference standards. The authors noted it had never been studied in humans, so its stimulant and addictive effects were unknown, and urged regulators to warn consumers and remove it from supplements.[2]

Uralets and colleagues reported in the Journal of Analytical Toxicology (2014) that 42 US urine samples screening positive for amphetamines in a three-month period in 2013 contained DEPEA and a related amine, and linked the supplement Craze to the supply of the compound.[9] A 2015 Polish study found it in 14 of 17 supplements tested, none listing it, and followed excretion in three volunteers, with detection lasting roughly two to five days.[10]

Press coverage in October and November 2013 included Nutraingredients reporting that the manufacturer of Craze disputed NSF's finding, USA Today reporting that Craze and Detonate contained a methamphetamine-like compound, and the New Zealand Herald reporting a warning issued over Craze.[1] New Zealand's regulator warning is dated November 2013.[1]

Legal status listed on Wikipedia includes Schedule I in Canada, Class A in the UK, Class C in New Zealand and a German NpSG listing for scientific and industrial use only.[1] Wikipedia describes it as sold as a designer drug.[1] The Wikipedia article does not describe US FDA action.

Supplement-contamination researchers place DEPEA within a wider pattern of undeclared stimulants in sports supplements. A 2020 narrative review describes how supplements can contain undeclared doping agents and cause unintentional anti-doping violations, and recommends athlete education and risk databases.[11] Wikipedia lists no reported poisonings, hospitalisations or deaths tied to the compound.[1]

No studies found. The compound has been tested only in analytical, animal and laboratory work: rat neurochemical and cardiovascular experiments,[3] enzyme-inhibition assays,[7][8] and rat self-administration.[4]

lore.intro: DEPEA is not discussed in forums as a compound people seek out. It circulates in supplement-safety coverage, anti-doping analysis and pre-workout discussion because of the 2013 findings in Craze and Detonate.[1][2]
